title: Lord's Supper
summary: Lord's Supper is a new covenant practice that marks initiation, remembrance, and communal identity in the church.
historical_context: The Synoptic passion narratives and First Corinthians preserve related but distinct meal traditions. First Corinthians embeds the received words within a conflict over unequal access, hunger, humiliation, and communal discernment.
ancient_near_east_context: The immediate context is Jewish festival and Greco-Roman communal dining rather than generalized ancient ritual.
hebraic_worldview: Blessing, shared bread and cup, covenant memory, Passover chronology, table fellowship, and responsibility for other participants shape the meal traditions.
second_temple_context: The Synoptic meals occur in a Jewish festival setting, though their chronology and relationship to Passover differ from John. Early assemblies also ate within hierarchical Roman households and cities.
canonical_context: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and First Corinthians transmit meal words with variations. First Corinthians 10-11 connects participation in Christ with rejection of rival cultic tables and correction of class humiliation.
literary_context: Gospels and epistles use Lord's Supper to connect Jesus' work to church practice.
covenantal_significance: Lord's Supper signals that the people of God now live in the fulfillment of the covenant in Christ.
canonical_role: Lord's Supper serves as an institutional anchor, connecting social practice, worship, leadership, and covenant life across related passages and themes.

related_objects.notes: The Corinth cluster supplies bounded banquet, association, hunger, and status comparisons for First Corinthians 11.
